# LESSONS — every عبرت line in the pool, with its source card

**This file is generated.** Run `python tools/promote_catalogue.py` after any research pass.

`CLAUDE.md` §0.2 — the catalogue is what artifacts read from; the research notes are the working
record. A سبق line that exists only inside a research note cannot be found when a later session
needs it, and two sessions end up drawing the same lesson in different words.

**Each line is drawn from the event itself.** None draws a present-day political parallel
(`DECISIONS.md` #26) — with an organisation in the room, the speaker narrates and does not
adjudicate. A deck uses at most **six** on its closing screen.


**1834 lines across 37 blocks.**

## الحسن ؓ, the handover, and عام الجماعة

| Card | Tier | عبرت |

| `TCO/E-HS1` | CORE | A man who has the power to decide the future may still judge that the community's own choosing is safer than his choosing for it. |

| `TCO/E-HS18` | CORE | When the argument is easy, the only thing being tested is the man. |

| `TCO/E-HS22` | GOOD | The same object can appear in two books and carry two different endings; a careful reader reports both and settles neither. |

| `TCO/E-HS24` | CORE | The men who can see a battle most clearly are usually the men who have fought in many. |
| `TCO/E-HS25` | CORE | A ruler's first question about a battle he can win is what will be left of the people afterwards. |
| `TCO/E-HS26` | GOOD | An envoy sent with room to agree can end a war that an envoy sent with demands will prolong. |
| `TCO/E-HS27` | CORE | A man who begins by naming what his own family has received is in a position to be believed about everything else. |
| `TCO/E-HS28` | GOOD | When both sides have already decided, the terms take an afternoon. |
| `TCO/E-HS29` | CORE | The cost of a long quarrel is not counted in battles; it is counted in roads, in kinship, and in borders nobody is watching. |
| `TCO/E-HS30` | GOOD | A decision made alone is a risk; a decision confirmed by one trusted man in the room is a position. |
| `TCO/E-HS31` | CORE | Honest men can look at the same facts and see two different duties. |
| `TCO/E-HS32` | CORE | A disagreement ends well when one of the two decides that the relationship is worth more than the argument. |
| `TCO/E-HS33` | GOOD | The man carrying the responsibility usually knows something the man advising him does not. |
| `TCO/E-HS34` | CORE | A historian who states a verdict and then names his evidence is doing the reader a service; the evidence is the part that matters. |
| `TCO/E-HS35` | CORE | A settlement written down in specific figures is a settlement somebody intended to keep. |
| `TCO/E-HS36` | CORE | When two independent books give the same three items, you are as close to the document as history lets you get. |
| `TCO/E-HS37` | CORE | Three books that agree on the shape of an agreement and differ on its items are telling you the document itself is gone. |
| `TCO/E-HS38` | GOOD | A clause that was never tested proves nothing about the men who wrote it. |
| `TCO/E-HS39` | GOOD | Numbers in old books drift; the safest thing to say aloud is the spread, not the figure. |
| `TCO/E-HS40` | CUT | Where the sources we trust contradict each other outright, the honest course is to say so and stop. |

| `TCO/E-HS46` | GOOD | The first man to give the allegiance was the last man to give it up — and he gave it up in the open, not by slipping away. |
| `TCO/E-HS47` | CORE | A man handed a blank page asked for nothing on it except protection for other people. |
| `TCO/E-HS48` | CORE | The willingness to fight is not the same thing as the willingness to fight now. |
| `TCO/E-HS49` | GOOD | The ablest men of a generation can end up on opposite sides of the same quarrel. |
| `TCO/E-HS50` | CORE | A ruler who can laugh at the title he has just been denied is telling you something about himself. |
| `TCO/E-HS51` | CORE | A plan to humiliate a man in public is a plan that can only be tested in public. |
| `TCO/E-HS52` | CORE | He answered the plan against him by saying the truest thing in the room and sitting down. |
| `TCO/E-HS53` | GOOD | Bad advice is remembered by the man who took it. |
| `TCO/E-HS54` | GOOD | He named his own standing first, so that nobody could say he had given away what he did not understand the value of. |
| `TCO/E-HS55` | CORE | He called the difference a difference, not a crime, and named his own reason for ending it. |
| `TCO/E-HS56` | CORE | A city can love a man and still be the reason he leaves it. |
| `TCO/E-HS57` | CORE | A commander's hardest judgement is about his own side, and he is usually the last person allowed to say it aloud. |
| `TCO/E-HS58` | CORE | The man who is insulted for making peace is usually the only one in the conversation who has counted the dead. |
| `TCO/E-HS59` | CORE | A man who gave up power when he had it is not likely to scheme for it when he does not. |
| `TCO/E-HS60` | GOOD | The most useful thing a scholar writes is often the sentence in which he tells you not to rely on what he has just transmitted. |
| `TCO/E-HS61` | CORE | A turning point in history can be certain in substance and uncertain in date, and both are worth saying aloud. |
| `TCO/E-HS62` | CORE | Notice that the disagreement about the number is not a disagreement about the event; it follows from the disagreement about the date. |
| `TCO/E-HS63` | GOOD | The most precise figure in a set of figures is not automatically the most reliable one. |

| `TCO/E-HS65` | GOOD | A historian who writes "the well-known view is" is telling you there is another one. |
| `TCO/E-HS66` | CORE | The arithmetic is the whole point: the thirty years close on the day this one young man steps down. |
| `TCO/E-HS67` | CORE | A change in what an office is called is sometimes the most honest record of what has changed about it. |

## The people: profiles I — عثمان ؓ's circle and the men of الجمل

| Card | Tier | عبرت |
|---|---|---|
| `POT/E-PF1` | CORE | A man's place in a quarrel is often decided by his family long before it is decided by his opinion. |
| `POT/E-PF2` | GOOD | A title the ummah remembers is worth more than one we would have invented, even when the chain that carries it is thin. |
| `POT/E-PF3` | GOOD | The suspicion a leader owes it to his brother to speak aloud is better out in the open than left to grow. |
| `POT/E-PF4` | CORE | What a man does on the worst day of his life is the fact about him that should be told first. |
| `POT/E-PF5` | GOOD | Some services are paid for once and then carried in the body for the rest of a life. |
| `POT/E-PF6` | GOOD | A man is credited with the good he intended and was kept from, not only with the good he was present for. |
| `POT/E-PF7` | CORE | Wealth is a trust that presses on the man who holds it, not a comfort he is owed. |
| `POT/E-PF8` | GOOD | The counsel that unties a knot often comes from inside the house, not from the assembly. |
| `POT/E-PF9` | GOOD | A claim of kinship that has never been used is the one that should be honoured most carefully. |
| `POT/E-PF10` | GOOD | Regular giving, fixed to the harvest and never announced, is a harder discipline than one large gift. |
| `POT/E-PF11` | CORE | A man who names his own failing before anyone else names it has already begun to answer for it. |
| `POT/E-PF12` | CORE | When the great scholars of the ummah have already chosen their words for a hard matter, using their words is safer than choosing our own. |
| `POT/E-PF13` | CORE | Men who send their own sons home before a march know what the march is. |
| `POT/E-PF14` | CORE | The men in that field were not strangers to each other, and that is exactly what made the day terrible. |
| `POT/E-PF15` | GOOD | A crowd that will not listen has already taken the decision out of the hands of the men it is following. |
| `POT/E-PF16` | CORE | In a fitna the deadliest arrow can come from a man's own side, which is one reason the books call such a day a fitna. |
| `POT/E-PF17` | CORE | The same measure applied to both sides is what makes a verdict trustworthy. |
| `POT/E-PF18` | CORE | Men who fought each other that morning were still brothers to each other that evening, and the books never pretended otherwise. |
| `POT/E-PF19` | GOOD | A quarrel among elders is paid for by young men who were never part of it. |
| `POT/E-PF20` | CUT | A number nobody checked travels further than one that was checked, which is why the scholars checked them. |
| `POT/E-PF21` | GOOD | A book that records its own uncertainty is more trustworthy than one that records only a single tidy answer. |
| `POT/E-PF22` | CORE | A man's standing in this story is established by the titles the ummah already gave him, not by any we might reach for. |
| `POT/E-PF23` | CORE | A man who answers the third time as readily as the first is the one worth sending. |
| `POT/E-PF24` | GOOD | Closeness of blood did not excuse a man from the errand; it was usually what got him sent. |
| `POT/E-PF25` | GOOD | A disposition shows itself early and does not change; the books simply record where it first showed. |
| `POT/E-PF26` | CORE | Men who begin together can still end on opposite sides of a field, and that is what makes a fitna a fitna. |
| `POT/E-PF27` | GOOD | Everything the room will hear tonight grew out of a community that once fielded two horses. |
| `POT/E-PF28` | GOOD | The errand nobody volunteers for is the one that decides the day. |
| `POT/E-PF29` | GOOD | The body of one Companion can carry the whole first forty years of this history on it. |
| `POT/E-PF30` | GOOD | There is a way of registering dissent that costs the man himself and costs nobody else anything. |
| `POT/E-PF31` | GOOD | What a man says of another when there is nothing to be gained by saying it is the testimony worth keeping. |
| `POT/E-PF32` | CORE | The office nobody campaigns for is given to the man everyone has already decided to trust. |
| `POT/E-PF33` | GOOD | Income a man refuses to let through his own door is the plainest test of what he thinks it is for. |
| `POT/E-PF34` | GOOD | A man who has already settled with himself how he expects to die is not easily governed by warnings. |
| `POT/E-PF35` | CORE | The warnings a community recites for years are usually understood to be about somebody else. |
| `POT/E-PF36` | GOOD | A man on the morning of a battle worries about the debts he owes, not about the argument he is in. |
| `POT/E-PF37` | CORE | A man who will change his mind in front of an army on the strength of one remembered sentence is a man who feared the sentence more than the army. |
| `POT/E-PF38` | CORE | It takes more courage to be called a coward by your own son than to ride into the line. |
| `POT/E-PF39` | GOOD | Withdrawing from a wrong does not guarantee safety; it only settles what a man will answer for. |
| `POT/E-PF40` | CORE | The men of that generation grieved for the men they had just been opposite, and the books recorded the grief as carefully as the fighting. |
| `POT/E-PF41` | GOOD | The head of a victorious army calling his opponent's killer a man of the Fire tells the room exactly how that day was understood at the time. |
| `POT/E-PF42` | GOOD | A refusal to take a revenge that was available is a fact about a man's judgement of worth, not about his weakness. |

| `POT/E-PF46` | GOOD | A man who refuses to hold money on terms that could leave the owner unpaid will die owing a fortune and leaving no one cheated. |
| `POT/E-PF47` | GOOD | An author who tells you which of two reports he prefers, and why, has given you more than one who gives you a single confident number. |
| `POT/E-PF48` | CORE | A person's standing is fixed by what they knew and taught, and it is not cancelled by one journey they later regretted. |
| `POT/E-PF49` | CORE | Most of what looks like faction in this year is family, and saying so plainly removes more heat than any argument would. |
| `POT/E-PF50` | GOOD | A distinction that came from God is not a grievance to be settled among people. |
| `POT/E-PF51` | CORE | The two names at the centre of this history were named together, and by the Prophet ﷺ himself. |
| `POT/E-PF52` | GOOD | Honour of this kind is reported plainly in the books, without ornament, and that is how it should be repeated. |
| `POT/E-PF53` | CORE | A charge answered from above needs no advocate below. |
| `POT/E-PF54` | GOOD | A ruler who departs from his own rule and says plainly why is easier to trust than one who hides the exception. |
| `POT/E-PF55` | CORE | When a position can be stated in two clauses, stating it in twenty is already an argument rather than a report. |
| `POT/E-PF56` | CORE | A warning given years in advance is only recognised at the moment it is too late to be convenient. |
| `POT/E-PF57` | CORE | The moment a person tries to turn back and is talked out of it is worth more attention than everything that follows it. |
| `POT/E-PF58` | CORE | Choosing not to narrate something is itself a scholarly judgement, and it can be followed as faithfully as any report. |
| `POT/E-PF59` | CORE | How the winner behaves in the first hour after winning is the part of a battle worth remembering. |
| `POT/E-PF60` | CORE | Regret that lasts a lifetime and is never argued about is the most convincing kind. |
| `POT/E-PF61` | CORE | A person who imposes a cost on herself for something nobody had charged her with has settled the matter more completely than any tribunal could. |
| `POT/E-PF62` | CORE | Repentance and good intention are not rival explanations; the tradition holds both at once and so should the platform. |
| `POT/E-PF63` | GOOD | The longest part of a life is often the teaching that came after the events everybody argues about. |
| `POT/E-PF64` | GOOD | A city that turns out at night, carrying its own light, is telling you what it thought it had lost. |
| `POT/E-PF65` | GOOD | A shrine in the wrong city is not piety, and the scholars said so in one sentence. |
| `POT/E-PF66` | GOOD | A man with no famous title can still be the one the community hands its hardest decision to. |
| `POT/E-PF67` | CORE | A man who would rather be shown the market than given the money has already told you what he will do with a fortune. |
| `POT/E-PF68` | GOOD | The men who financed this community were the same men who bled for it, and the two facts belong in the same sentence. |
| `POT/E-PF69` | GOOD | Rank in that community was never a claim about the man; it was simply where he happened to be standing when the prayer began. |
| `POT/E-PF70` | CORE | A community that has to decide whose memory to trust is already doing the work that later became a science. |
| `POT/E-PF71` | GOOD | The administration of an empire was being built out of remembered sentences, one testimony at a time. |
| `POT/E-PF72` | CORE | The sifting of reports did not begin with the scholars; it began with the caliphs, in the Companions' own lifetimes. |
| `POT/E-PF73` | CORE | The only way to be trusted with a decision of that size is to have removed yourself from its benefits first. |
| `POT/E-PF74` | GOOD | The man who understands what an office costs is the one least eager to be given it. |
| `POT/E-PF75` | GOOD | An argument dressed up as piety is still an argument, and it can be refused outright. |
| `POT/E-PF76` | CORE | The proof that a decision was fair is usually the person who did not get it. |
| `POT/E-PF77` | GOOD | The rich man who is frightened of his own money is the one who can be trusted with it. |
| `POT/E-PF78` | GOOD | A caliph who accepts a legacy on the same footing as any other man of Badr is telling the city what the office is not. |
| `POT/E-PF79` | CORE | Some men are taken before the hard years arrive, and the generation left behind knows exactly what that means. |
| `POT/E-PF80` | CORE | Kinship in this story is never decoration; it is usually the thing that explains the decision. |
| `POT/E-PF81` | CORE | Every movement that later filled continents was once small enough for one man to be a third of it. |
| `POT/E-PF82` | GOOD | A generation that arrives after the hard years often assumes it is qualified to grade the people who lived through them. |
| `POT/E-PF83` | GOOD | Praise of that weight was given for service rendered under arrows, not for anything said in an assembly. |
| `POT/E-PF84` | GOOD | The man who turns up unasked in the dark is the one the wish was about. |
| `POT/E-PF85` | CORE | Being complained about is not by itself evidence of anything, and a careful ruler checks before he concludes. |
| `POT/E-PF86` | CORE | The best answer to a complaint is a plain account of what was actually done. |
| `POT/E-PF87` | GOOD | A ruler may think well of a man and still check the complaint, and doing both is what makes the good opinion worth having. |
| `POT/E-PF88` | CORE | Most of what looks like a slight is a man occupied with something else, and the fastest way to know is to ask him. |
| `POT/E-PF89` | GOOD | A quarrel between two of the best men of the ummah was ended in one sitting because both of them wanted it ended. |
